stories.headline: White House replaces national cyber director after a run of tech outages
stories.summary: National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is out of his post, and President Trump has named Pentagon chief information officer Kirsten Davies as acting cyber chief. The change follows a series of technology outages that disrupted air travel, banking and national security systems. Separately, the FBI is reported to be investigating an apparent breach of its national crime database.
stories.why_it_matters: The outages grounded flights and delayed bank payments for ordinary customers, and the person coordinating the federal response to such failures has just changed. Whether the outages are connected, and what caused them, has not been established.
stories.background: The national cyber director is the White House's top adviser on cybersecurity policy; the Senate confirmed Cairncross to the job in August 2025. Over roughly ten days in November, a string of failures hit major systems: a timeline compiled by TechRepublic lists a nationwide FAA ground stop on Nov. 13, a JPMorgan Chase payments problem on Nov. 16 and a Microsoft 365 email disruption. The FAA and JPMorgan each said they had found no sign of a cyberattack, according to that timeline. Stephen Miller recently became White House chief of staff. Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the midterms and take over in January, which affects how quickly a permanent successor could be confirmed.

The change came days after outages disrupted U.S. air travel, banking and national security systems.

The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center, a database that federal and local law enforcement use to share information, according to two people briefed on the matter who spoke to NBC News. CNN first reported the breach.
Lawmakers quoted by Fox News said power grids, water systems and banks are vulnerable after what the outlet called a 10-day wave of outages.

The FAA said it had no indication that a cyberattack caused its Nov. 13 ground stop, and JPMorgan Chase said it found no evidence of one in its Nov. 16 payments problem, according to a TechRepublic timeline.

stories.headline: Senate passes bipartisan bill to speed energy and infrastructure permits
stories.summary: The Senate voted 62-33 on Thursday night to pass a bill that overhauls federal permitting rules for power plants, transmission lines and other energy and infrastructure projects. The bill, which President Trump backs, also requires data centers to pay for energy costs. It now goes to the House.

Lawmakers from both parties have tried for several years to shorten that process. Senators reached a bipartisan deal on this bill in the fall, and it cleared a 73-25 procedural vote on Nov. 9, according to Axios. Electricity demand from data centers has grown quickly and became an issue in this month's midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of Congress starting in January.

stories.headline: Trump defends calling Putin a friend at lengthy post-summit news conference
stories.summary: Back from a three-way summit in China with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, President Trump held a long White House news conference on Friday. He defended calling Putin his friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the United States, and said Iran would not make an "acceptable" deal to end the war. stories.background: Trump met Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China, this week in the first three-way meeting of the leaders. Russia has been at war in Ukraine since 2022, and the U.S. is engaged in a war with Iran that Democrats in Congress want to end. stories.summary: A federal jury in Los Angeles on Friday found Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, guilty of two arson charges for starting the blaze that became the January 2025 Palisades Fire. stories.headline: Myanmar rejects UN court's finding that it committed genocide against the Rohingya
stories.summary: The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority, in a case brought by Gambia. Myanmar's military-backed government called the ruling "unfair", and rights groups urged governments to impose sanctions. The court ordered reparations, safe return for those who fled and prosecutions, but it has no way to enforce the ruling.
stories.why_it_matters: It is reported to be the first time the UN's top court has held a state responsible for genocide, and analysts quoted in the coverage say the way the court judged intent could shape other genocide cases, including the one against Israel. For Rohingya refugees, little changes soon, because the court cannot enforce its orders.
stories.background: The Rohingya are a mostly Muslim minority from Myanmar, many of whom fled to neighbouring Bangladesh to escape military violence and still live in refugee camps there. Gambia brought a case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice in 2019 under the 1948 Genocide Convention, and the court ruled in 2022 that it had jurisdiction. The ICJ, based in The Hague, settles disputes between states; it does not try individuals. Its rulings are binding, but it has no enforcement arm, so a state that believes a ruling is being ignored can turn to the UN Security Council.

facts.text: The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday, Nov. 19, that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya.
The ruling orders Myanmar to let those who fled return home safely, to pay reparations to the Rohingya and to prosecute people suspected of genocide; the court has no power to enforce it.
The judges decided for Gambia by nine votes to six, and reports describe it as the first time the court has held a state responsible for genocide.
The amount of compensation is to be set in later proceedings, and the judgment does not order Myanmar to grant the Rohingya citizenship.
Myanmar dismissed the ruling as "unfair".
Rights groups urged governments to impose sanctions on Myanmar after the ruling.
Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh welcomed the verdict but told the AP they want to go home to Myanmar.

stories.headline: S&P 500 and Dow fall into correction as the sell-off in AI stocks deepens
stories.summary: The S&P 500 fell 3.7% on Friday, and both it and the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed in correction territory, meaning at least 10% below their record highs. The Nasdaq composite gave up its gain for 2026 and, according to MarketWatch, had its worst week since 2020. Chipmakers led the declines, and shares of Anthropic slid on their second day of trading after the largest IPO on record.
stories.why_it_matters: Most retirement accounts and index funds hold large positions in the technology companies leading this decline, so a correction shows up directly in 401(k) and savings balances. Outlets across the spectrum covered the drop.
stories.background: A handful of very large technology companies tied to artificial intelligence drove most of the stock market's gains this year, and because of their size they weigh heavily on the main indexes. Since early November investors have been selling those shares amid questions about whether the heavy spending on AI chips and data centers will pay off. Oil prices rose sharply because of the war involving Iran, and the administration argues that this kind of supply shock should not be met with rate increases. stories.headline: Amazon's campaign against delivery worker bill is straining ties with Council speaker
stories.summary: Gothamist reports that Council Speaker Julie Menin is growing frustrated with Amazon as the company steps up lobbying against a Council bill covering delivery workers who work for its contractors. Amazon this week began warning customers in its app that the bill could raise order costs. Other reports say lawmakers are weighing changes to the bill, with a vote possible in the coming weeks.
stories.why_it_matters: The bill would change how thousands of package delivery workers in the city are employed, and Amazon says it could make orders cost more, a claim the speaker rejects. Only Gothamist among ingested outlets covered this today.
stories.background: Many drivers who deliver Amazon packages wear its branding but are employed by smaller contractor firms. The Delivery Protection Act, a Council bill backed by the Teamsters union and Mayor Zohran Mamdani, would regulate that arrangement and the warehouses packages leave from. Amazon opposes it; earlier reporting by New York Focus said the company funded a multimillion-dollar lobbying campaign against it. Speaker Julie Menin controls whether and when the bill gets a vote and has said she is working through legal issues with it.

stories.headline: Bronx funeral held for Javits Frimpong, 15, as prosecutors describe the shooting
stories.summary: A large crowd, including Mayor Zohran Mamdani, attended the funeral Friday of Javits Frimpong, the 15-year-old shot dead on his way to school in the Bronx last month. The Rev. Al Sharpton gave the eulogy. Prosecutors said the teens who killed him took turns shooting, the Daily News reported; one 17-year-old has been charged and police have said they are looking for two others.
stories.why_it_matters: The killing of a student walking to school has become a focus of the city's debate over youth gun violence, and two suspects have not been arrested. Ingested coverage is from left-leaning and center outlets only.
stories.background: Javits Frimpong, a 10th grader who had come from Ghana, was shot on Oct. 29 while walking to school in the Bronx. Police arrested a 17-year-old in November and charged him with murder; the Bronx district attorney's office is prosecuting. The family is represented by civil rights attorney Ben Crump and has been supported by Sharpton's National Action Network. Early reports linked the shooting to bullying, but Crump has said prosecutors told the family the shooters did not attend Frimpong's school; amNY describes the killing as a case of mistaken identity.

stories.headline: Group files new petitions to open city primaries to all voters
stories.summary: Unite NY, a group that wants every registered voter to be able to vote in city primaries, has submitted a second batch of petitions to put the question on the ballot, Gothamist reports. Its first batch was rejected by the city and is still in court. Mayor Zohran Mamdani has pushed back on the effort.
stories.why_it_matters: Voters not enrolled in a party cannot vote in the primaries that usually decide who wins city offices; a ballot question could change that for the next mayoral election. Only Gothamist among ingested outlets covered this.
stories.background: New York City has closed primaries: only voters registered with a party can vote in that party's primary. Because Democrats far outnumber Republicans in the city, the Democratic primary often decides the winner. Unite NY is using a petition process to try to put a charter change on the ballot instead of going through a mayor-appointed charter revision commission. It filed about 45,000 signatures in July; the city clerk found too few were valid, and the group sued. Mamdani has said he is content with the current primary system.

markets.summary: U.S. stocks fell sharply on Friday, ending what a CNN headline called the worst week for the market in over a year. The S&P 500 sank 3.7% and the Nasdaq, which is heavy with technology companies, lost more than 1,200 points and is now down for the year, the Associated Press and CBS News reported. The S&P 500 and the Dow both closed in a correction, the term for a drop of at least 10% from a recent high. The selling was led by chipmakers and other companies tied to artificial intelligence; shares of Anthropic, the Claude maker that went public on Thursday, slid on their second day but stayed above their offering price, MarketWatch reported. Reuters reported that investors moved money into "value" stocks, meaning cheaper shares of established companies, and that bitcoin fell to its lowest level in two years.

concept.explanation: A correction is Wall Street's word for a stock index or share price falling at least 10% from its most recent peak; a fall of 20% or more is called a bear market. Corrections happen when investors decide prices ran ahead of what companies are likely to earn, or when something makes them less willing to take risks, such as higher interest rates or doubts about a hot sector like AI. They are fairly common and often reverse within months, though some turn into deeper declines. If you own stock funds in a 401(k) or IRA, a correction shows up as a lower balance, which matters most if you need to sell soon; for people still saving, it also means new contributions buy shares at lower prices.
